title: Surgical separation of prefetch reservation and tokenization pipeline to reduce KV contention
creator: Sophie Chen
description:
Problem:

The current serving runtime couples tokenization, prefetch reservation, and slot allocation in a single synchronous request pipeline. That coupling creates several operational issues under real workloads: head-of-line jitter when tokenization stalls, long-held scheduler locks during prefetch reservations, and KV-cache thrash when many concurrent requests attempt to prime identical hotkeys. These manifest as elevated P95/P99 token generation latency and CPU contention during synthetic and customer workloads with high short-lived concurrency.

Goal:

Split the tokenization step out of the reservation/slot allocation critical path and introduce a lease-less, lightweight prefetch reservation that does not require holding scheduler locks. The change should reduce contention on the scheduler and KV-cache, lower tail latencies under bursty traffic, and simplify future batching optimizations. This is a focused tech-debt refactor — no model-serving semantics change expected.

Proposed approach:

1. Introduce an asynchronous tokenization stage: tokenization runs in an isolated worker pool and returns a tokenization token (opaque handle) instead of blocking the slot allocator.
2. Implement a lease-less prefetch reservation API: callers obtain a small, TTL-bound reservation token that represents a prefetch intent. Reservation tokens do not acquire global scheduler locks and are recorded in a compact in-memory prefetch ledger per-shard.
3. Move hotkey prefetch accounting into a probabilistic admission controller per KV shard. Use a lightweight token-bucket fed by observed request rates to limit simultaneous prefetches for a given hotkey window.
4. Ensure the slot allocator consumes tokenization tokens and reservation tokens independently, allowing slot allocation to proceed without long tokenization waits while still preserving correctness for KV priming.
5. Add migration shims so older runtime nodes continue to interoperate during a rolling upgrade (reservation tokens degrade to synchronous path if peer does not understand the token).

Trade-offs and rationale:

- Pros: reduces lock contention, shortens critical path latency, reduces repeated prefetching of identical KV entries, and enables independent scaling of tokenization and reservation subsystems.
- Cons: added complexity in bookkeeping (reservation ledger + TTLs), potential for slightly higher memory usage while reservation tokens are live, and need for robust rollout and fallback to prevent correctness regressions.

Observability & safety:

- Emit metrics: reservation_token_issued, reservation_token_expired, prefetch_blocked_by_admission, reservation_fallback_sync, tokenization_queue_depth.
- Add distributed tracing spans for tokenization and reservation lifecycles to analyze cross-service latencies.
- Provide feature-flag gated rollout with canary (10%) -> ramp (50%) -> global (100%) and automatic fallback on elevated error or latency alarms.

Acceptance criteria:
acceptance_criteria: Unit and integration tests for reservation API and tokenization token lifecycle
End-to-end correctness: priming still ensures required KV state is available before first model call in canary tests
Benchmark: P99 generation latency decreases by >= 15% under bursty 200qps short-lived sessions compared to baseline
Scheduler CPU contention reduced: top-of-pipeline lock hold time reduced by >= 40% in perf harness
No more than 5% increase in steady-state memory footprint for serving hosts
Rollout plan documented with automatic fallback triggers and runbook entries
Security review completed for new reservation token mechanism and in-memory ledger (KMS/PII considerations)
